It's not that the debt can't be discharged that's the problem. It's all the shady, underhanded, borderline criminal tactics they use to get their money back that's the problem.

  • Student takes out loan from <BigBank>'s student loan program and uses it to pay for college
  • Bank sells that debt off to another loan servicing company
  • Loan servicing company packages that debt with hundreds or thousands of others, then sells that package to yet another company
  • This company may also repackage and sell on the debt
  • Student graduates from college, six months later, the payments start to come due
  • Economy goes to shit, student can't find a job to pay the loan back and live off of at the same time
  • Student defaults on said loan
  • Package containing said loan is sold off to a collection agency
  • Collection agency hounds the crap out of the student with borderline illegal letters and phone calls
  • Collection agency gives up, sells the debt to YET ANOTHER agency, who begins the collection process all over again

Every step of the way, records of ownership can and do get lost. Things like an accounting of amounts owed, payments made, chain of title for who owns the debt when, etc. The collection agencies are legally required to prove the debt is owed before they can collect one single cent. However, they rely on the borrower not knowing their rights, and the vague threats of legal action to coerce them into a repayment scheme that they may or may not be able to afford.

Then it can get ugly. The current holder of the loan (usually some massive trust who only has account numbers and names in a database, no other documentation) decides they need to collect on this current crop of debts. So they send out collection letters that basically amount to "you owe us because we say you do, pay up or get sued". Even if the borrower sends a demand for validation (which, legally, the alleged debt-owner MUST respond to, and they MUST cease all collection activities until they do so), the alleged debt-owner doesn't stop. They either ignore the validation demand, or respond with a "we checked with ourselves, and we're sure this information is correct, now pay up" form letter, which satisfies the "verification" clause of the FDCPA, but won't ever hold up in court. The phone calls continue before that letter is even sent (also against the law). Even better, they use actual law firms (that may or may not be licensed in the student-borrower's state to even practice law) to do the collection services, to make people think "this is from a legal firm, I better pay up or I'll get sued."

Or they ignore the demand for validation completely, and just go straight to filing a lawsuit of a whopping three paragraphs:

1. Plaintiff is the holder of a Contract executed by the Defendant on <Date>. A copy of the said contract is attached hereto and incorporated herein.

2. The amount due and owing on the Contract is $<amount> plus accrued interest of $<otheramount>

*3. Although due demand has been made, the Defendants have failed to liquidate the balance due and owing.

That's it. They then include a heavily redacted and horribly degraded copy of a fax of a printout with the borrower's supposed signature, and half a ream of bullshit that's really just boilerplate text for any given loan, not actual documentation of amounts/payments/interest charges/etc. that must be proven. This is the point where they're hoping people will give in and start begging "omgplz drop the lawsuit I'll pay I'll pay!" despite having shown no proof that this 5th party organization that nobody has ever heard of is actually the one who owns the alleged debt (and whose name never appears on ANY originating documents).

That's where they make their money. The original lender has LONG SINCE been paid when they sold off the debt along with thousands of others. The student borrower is now facing a weaponized lawsuit to extract money from them so someone that can't or won't prove they even own the debt can get a payday. They've likely paid pennies on the dollar for the debt at this point, but want the full amount PLUS usurious interest to "make them whole."

So say the student-borrower calls their bluff and fires back a response and a counter-suit for any number of violations of federal debt collection laws committed during this process. The shady company simply fires back with boilerplate defenses like "hurrrr, we're not an actual debt collector, so the FDCPA doesn't apply to us, and even if we did, we're protected by the "we didn't mean to" clause!" (Seriously, "bona fide error" is an actual defense, even though the FDCPA is technically a strict-liability statute.

This drags on and on, while the slimeball company hopes to exhaust the borrowers money and/or willpower so they finally give up and sell a kidney to pay off the debt at a "significantly reduced" settlement price, which is still probably 50x more than they paid for a file with a couple names and numbers to begin with.

tl;dr - Student loans themselves aren't the problem. The industry surrounding the buying/selling/collecting of those debts, however, is corrupt to the core and full of bottom-feeding shitbrains looking to make money by intimidating people. If someone can give you ample evidence (i.e. leaves no legal doubt) that they do, in fact, own the debt you took out, then pay them. If they can't or won't prove it, they can go fuck themselves with a goddamn AIDS-covered cactus.

This is really some serious advice. I see questions about debt in general all the time on /r/personalfinance (yeah, it's Reddit, but it's a good community), and seriously just asking for validation of debt can get someone off the hook because companies are careless with maintaining records. It's amazing that in the digital age information is so easily lost, but I guess the prevalent use of hard copy paperwork in the business world keeps this going.

(Obligatory IANAL, this is not legal advice, etc.)

Mailing them a demand for validation letter within the 30 day period is always a good idea, IMO, even if you're 100% sure the debt is legit. Not only is it your legal right to do so, but it also puts them on notice that you're aware of your rights and will make sure they're respected.

I've had to send one or two in my day, and mine is usually something similar to the following:

<Address of Collection Agency>

Re: <File/Account #XXX>

To Whom It May Concern,

I am in receipt of your communication dated <date of their collection letter> in regards to the account(s) referenced above. Per 15 USC § 1692g (b), I hereby dispute the validity of the claimed debt(s), and demand full and complete written validation of the same.

This validation shall include (but not be limited to):

  • The name and address of the original creditor.

  • Certified copies of the signed instruments creating the claimed debt(s).

  • Certified copies of the signed agreement(s) between your organization and the original creditor, verifying you are authorized to collect these amounts.

  • A full accounting of the amounts requested and how they were calculated, including a full listing of payments made to the original creditor, a full listing of payments made to any other parties acting on behalf of the original creditor (including collection agencies, if applicable), and a full listing of any and all interest/fees associated with the requested amounts.

Please provide the requested validation within 30 days of receipt of this letter. If no validation is provided, or if validation is incomplete, I will assume the aforementioned communication was received in error.

Then you send this via certified mail, so you know EXACTLY when they get it and who received it. That way, if they file suit anyway, they can't claim they didn't get a validation letter. And filing suit without responding to the letter? That comes under "failing to cease all collection activities until such time as the demand has been responded to" and is another FDCPA violation.

The kicker, however, is that per the FDCPA, all they really have to do is "verify" the debt. That usually means they send you the form letter with "well, we checked with our people, and asked ourselves if it was correct, and we told us that it was, so you owe us." Technically, that satisfies responding to your demand for validation. But sending such a thorough request puts them on notice that if they do take you to court, you will make damn sure they have to prove it to the court's satisfaction. And "we told ourselves it was right" does NOT meet the "preponderance of evidence" standard.

Bottom line, document EVERY. SINGLE. COMMUNICATION. Save letters. Save voicemails they leave you, etc. If they try to screw you over after all of that, chances are you can easily find a lawyer who will take your case on a contingency basis.

For those who would ask "if you know you owe someone money, why not just pay it?" I respond with this: If they can't be bothered to keep accurate records to prove you owe the money to them, what assurance do you have that they'll keep accurate records of your payments? Yes, payments "going missing" after the check gets to their office does happen, and they do use that to cause whatever payment arrangement you made to become null and void, which they will happily use to go back to the court and get a default judgment against you, using the court to force you to pay the entire amount immediately, plus whatever they "kindly discounted" to get the payment plan, plus their legal fees, etc. So "document everything" applies to payments as well. You should also be sending those via certified mail. More expensive, but worth the peace of mind.

And finally, if you're getting harassed by a collector for a debt that isn't yours, you're telling them that they need to back off or get sued, and that it's their job to prove the debt is legit, not yours to prove it isn't.
